Adequacy of a fitted model, as tests

Source: R/ctFitAdequacy.R
ctFitAdequacy.Rd

Tests a fitted model in families, each aimed at one way a continuous time model can fall short, and gives each family a p-value. Most families use the one-step-ahead prediction errors, which under the model are independent and standard normal however the observations are spaced. Each variable's error is taken given the others observed at the same time, so a result can be tied to a variable.

Usage

ctFitAdequacy(
  fit,
  covariates = NULL,
  families = c("residuals", "latent", "volatility", "pairs", "periodic", "distribution",
    "fit", "dependence", "effects", "tvcovariates", "subjects", "nonlinear",
    "covariates"),
  gaps = NULL,
  periods = NULL,
  tvcovariates = NULL,
  close = 0.05,
  alpha = 0.05,
  projection = c("auto", "derivative", "plugin", "opg", "none"),
  parameters = NULL,
  nsamples = 100,
  lags = 0:3,
  nboot = 1999L,
  cores = getOption("mc.cores", 2L)
)

Arguments

fit

A fit from ctFit, either backend. The projection needs backend = 'julia'.

covariates

Optional subject level covariates, as for ctScoreTest, for the covariates family.

families

Which families to run; see Details. scores and lagged run only when named here.

gaps

Break points, in the data's time units, for the time gap bins of the residual correlations. By default the eighth, quarter and half quantiles of the time between every pair of a subject's rows.

periods

Periods, in the data's time units, for the periodic family, such as 24 for a daily cycle with time in hours. By default a range of periods is scanned.

tvcovariates

Optional time varying covariates for the tvcovariates family: a data frame with the model's subject id and time columns and one or more numeric columns, matched to the fit's rows by id and time.

close

The root mean square residual correlation regarded as a close fit.

alpha

Level for adequate and close_fit.

projection

How the tests based on the errors account for the estimation of the parameters. 'derivative' differentiates the statistics with respect to every parameter (two passes of the filter per parameter) and uses the fit's Hessian. 'plugin', on a Laplace fit, does the same more cheaply, with each subject's random effects estimated once from the whole record, and is approximate. 'opg' uses the outer product of the scores, which needs many more subjects than parameters. 'none' ignores estimation, which is conservative and can hide a strong misfit in the distribution family. When random effects affect the dynamics or the variances, 'derivative' and 'plugin' correct only the distribution, fit, effects and scores families. 'auto' (the default) takes the first that is affordable: 'derivative' when the fit has a Hessian and the passes take under getOption('ctsem.adequacy.budget', 120) seconds, then 'plugin' on the same terms, 'opg' with at least ten subjects per parameter, and otherwise 'none'.

parameters

For the scores family, the raw parameters whose row scores are used. By default up to 16 of the dynamic and measurement parameters, those in DRIFT, DIFFUSION and CINT first.

nsamples

Number of generated datasets, for the families that need them. Generated data already on fit are reused if there are enough.

lags

Observation lags for the lagged family.

nboot

Bootstrap draws for each family's calibration.

cores

Cores for the engine and for generating data.

Value

An object of class ctFitAdequacy, containing: families, one row per family with the number of statistics, the worst one, its z, the family's p-value and the Holm adjusted p-value; statistics, every statistic, with what it is about in the columns variable, with (the other variable of a pair, or what the variable is correlated with), gap (the time gap bin or lag), period and covariate, each NA where it does not apply, and its observed value, z and two-sided p; size, the root mean square residual correlations with their intervals and close fit tests; errors, the rows the error based families use, in long form, with Subject, Time, Element ('error' for each variable's standardised one-step-ahead error, 'update' for each latent's standardised update, 'etaprior' for its predicted mean), Row, the variable and value, or NULL when no such family ran; adequate; close_fit; informative, whether the tvcovariates predict the errors at alpha (NA without them); projection, the method used; degenerate, the axes the effects family left out; and fit, with any generated data, for reuse. plot() draws the families, or one family's statistics.

Details

residuals

Correlations between the errors of a subject's rows, for every pair of rows, by time gap (gaps): the residual autocorrelation and cross-correlation in continuous time. Slow structure missing from the model shows as correlation over the gaps it spans.

latent

The same for each latent process, using the standardised update each row makes to the predicted state. There is one set per process, so misfit in the dynamics is not diluted by item specific structure.

volatility

The same for the squared errors of each variable: variance that clusters in time.

pairs

The correlation of each pair of variables' errors in the same row, against the correlation the model implies. This detects a wrong measurement error covariance or loading.

periodic

A cycle missing from the model, such as a daily rhythm. Each variable's errors, and each latent's updates, are correlated with the same subject's at other times, weighted by the cosine of the time between them over the period. This is the periodogram of the errors at that period. It depends only on the time between rows, so it finds a cycle whatever its phase in each subject. It uses the given periods, or by default scans from twice the typical interval between rows to half the typical record length. The estimate is the errors' autocorrelation at the period, and a cycle with amplitude a, in error standard deviations, gives a^2 / 2.

distribution

Skewness and kurtosis of each variable's errors, and each row's squared standardised distance against the mean and variance of its chi-square distribution, with Anderson-Darling tests against the normal and chi-square.

fit

How unevenly subjects are fitted: the spread of each subject's summed distance against the chi-square's, and the worst subject.

dependence

The distance correlation of each variable's error, and of its square, with the predicted latent states, the previous errors and the time interval, tested by permutation. This detects a conditional mean or variance the model gets wrong, in any form.

effects

On a single level Laplace fit, whether a normal distribution suits the random effects. At cuts along each axis, each subject's smoothed posterior probability that its standardised effect lies below the cut is compared with the normal's. Under the model these differences have mean zero, and a skewed or bimodal distribution, or a subgroup, moves them (based on the gradient function of Verbeke & Molenberghs, 2013, and Drikvandi, Verbeke & Molenberghs, 2017). An effect the data leave at its prior in every subject is left out (degenerate). Fits with more than four random effects per subject are not tested, with a message.

tvcovariates

With tvcovariates, whether time varying variables not in the model predict its errors. Each variable's error, and each latent's update, is regressed on each standardised covariate at the same row and at the subject's previous row. The previous row tests prediction, in Granger's sense. The same row tests association, which also shows when the outcome itself moves the covariate. A correct model of the outcomes fails this test when a covariate is another measure of the same latent states, since it sharpens the estimate of the state. So a failure says that a model using these variables would predict better, and not that the model of the outcomes is wrong. This family is not counted in adequate.

scores

Run only when named in families. White's (1987) dynamic information matrix test: the score of each row's one-step log likelihood for the dynamic and measurement parameters (parameters), correlated with the scores of the same subject's other rows, by time gap. Under the model these are uncorrelated, so this checks for dynamic misspecification of any kind. Because it is so broad, it is the least powerful family, and ctScoreTest detects the departures it covers far more often. It can take hours on large data.

subjects, nonlinear, covariates, lagged

Statistics of the data compared with datasets generated from the fit: how much subjects differ in mean, standard deviation and lag one correlations, whether change depends nonlinearly on level, with covariates whether subjects' statistics depend on them, and the data's own lagged correlations (lags). These use the data twice and are conservative. The lagged correlations are usually reproduced by the fit, so lagged runs only when named in families.

The tests based on the errors account for the estimation of the parameters (projection), and take their variance from the errors themselves, so they hold with heavy tails or changing variance. The periodic statistics are skewed, and are referred to a chi-square matched to their skewness. The distribution and fit families use a studentised bootstrap over subjects. Within a family, the largest statistic and the sum of the squared statistics are each tested, taking the statistics' correlation into account, and combined with the Cauchy combination test. Families are combined by Holm's method, and adequate is TRUE when no family's adjusted p-value is below alpha. The tvcovariates family is left out of this, and its p-value is reported in informative.

On a Laplace fit (intoverpop = 'laplace') whose random effects affect the dynamics or the variances, each row's error comes from the model's predictive distribution given the subject's earlier rows, with the random effects integrated by importance sampling (getOption('ctsem.sequential.particles', 512) quasi-random draws per subject). The draws are fixed by getOption('ctsem.sequential.seed'), so a call can be repeated, and another seed or more draws shows how much of a result is due to the sampling. With random effects at more than one level this is not available, so the row distances are left out and the latent family's p-values are approximate, with a message.

For a binary, ordinal, count or censored item, the error is replaced by its randomised probability integral transform, mapped through the normal quantile function. Under the model these are independent standard normal, so every family uses them as it uses Gaussian errors. The latent family's updates on such rows rest on the filter's Gaussian approximation for the item, so its p-values are approximate there, with a message. The pairs family does not pair a non-Gaussian item with a Gaussian one.

With many observations every misfit becomes significant, so the size of the residual, latent and within row correlations the model leaves is reported too, as a bias corrected root mean square (as for the SRMR, Maydeu-Olivares 2017), with a 95 per cent interval and p_close, the p-value for the test that it is at least close. close_fit is TRUE when every failing family is one of these three, and each of their sizes is shown to be below close at alpha. A size whose interval reaches close is not a close fit. A close fit refers to these averages over many correlations, and one large discrepancy, or a biased estimate of a quantity of interest, can still hide under a small average.

A failure in one variable's equation also shows in the other variables' errors, so a failing statistic does not always point to where the problem is. ctScoreTest is more sensitive to the departures it covers, and ctModelImprove uses both.

References

Newey, W. K. (1985). Maximum likelihood specification testing and conditional moment tests. Econometrica, 53, 1047-1070.

White, H. (1987). Specification testing in dynamic models. In T. Bewley (Ed.), Advances in Econometrics: Fifth World Congress. Cambridge University Press.

Verbeke, G., & Molenberghs, G. (2013). The gradient function as an exploratory goodness-of-fit assessment of the random-effects distribution in mixed models. Biostatistics, 14, 477-490.

Drikvandi, R., Verbeke, G., & Molenberghs, G. (2017). Diagnosing misspecification of the random-effects distribution in mixed models. Biometrics, 73, 63-71.

Chang, J., Yao, Q., & Zhou, W. (2017). Testing for high-dimensional white noise using maximum cross-correlations. Biometrika, 104, 111-127.

Chen, S. X., & Qin, Y.-L. (2010). A two-sample test for high-dimensional data with applications to gene-set testing. The Annals of Statistics, 38, 808-835.

Liu, Y., & Xie, J. (2020). Cauchy combination test. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 115, 393-402.

Maydeu-Olivares, A. (2017). Assessing the size of model misfit in structural equation models. Psychometrika, 82, 533-558.

See also

ctPostPredPlots and ctFitCheckCov to see the data against the fit.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (isTRUE(ctJuliaStatus()$available)) {
model <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(2),
  manifestNames = c('Y1', 'Y2'), latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'),
  TDpredNames = 'TD1')
fit <- ctFit(ctsemtestdat, model, priors = TRUE)
adequacy <- ctFitAdequacy(fit)
print(adequacy)     # one row per family of tests
print(plot(adequacy))
}
# }
